title: Farmer's grain co-op: OEMs jointly own a take-or-pay DRAM fab
idea: Thinking like a Midwest grain cooperative, mid-size OEMs (PC, auto, telecom, tier-2 cloud) form a member-owned memory co-op that signs 7-year take-or-pay offtake for a 40k-wafer/month fab and pledges those contracts as collateral for project-finance debt. Members get bits at cost-plus with patronage dividends instead of paying spot prices.
why: Capital intensity and price volatility: turns $15B of equity risk into contract-backed debt at a cost of capital ~2-3 points lower, makes a new U.S. fab bankable, and shields members from 4x price spikes.

title: Embargo engineer's reballing brigade for e-waste phone LPDDR
idea: Like a Soviet engineer under embargo salvaging chips from Western hardware, automated lines pull LPDDR4X/LPDDR5 packages off scrapped phones and laptops (IR desolder, X-ray inspection, reball). Packages pass 48-hour march and retention screens and are mounted, graded, on CXL Type-3 carrier cards whose controller maps around weak banks.
why: Supply and scarce resources: ~1.2B phones a year retire with 4-12 GB each; recovering 10% gives ~1 EB/yr of DRAM-class capacity (a few % of world bit supply) with almost no fab capital.

title: Child asks why servers don't share: per-second rack memory market
idea: A child sees half of each server's RAM sitting idle and asks why they don't share. A CXL 3.x rack pool lends each host's stranded DRAM in 256 MB slices through a per-second internal auction run by the fabric manager, and reclaims a slice in under 100 ms by migrating its pages to a compressed tier.
why: Usable supply: hyperscaler DRAM utilization is ~50-60%; pooling plus a price signal could cut fleet DRAM purchases 15-25%, at ~200 ns extra latency on borrowed pages.

title: Biologist's apoptosis: sell dies with dead banks as smaller parts
idea: Cells die in a controlled way so the organism survives. Likewise, fuse off the failed banks or subarrays on DRAM dies that miss full spec and ship them as 12 Gb or 8 Gb 'harvested' parts, with a JEDEC capacity descriptor so controllers map only the live banks (GPU binning applied to memory).
why: Cost per bit and supply: recovers the ~5-15% of dies scrapped at wafer sort and burn-in, adding supply without a single new wafer.

title: Alien asks why three companies own memory: open DRAM PDK
idea: An alien surveying Earth finds a three-vendor oligopoly. The U.S. buys a full mature-node DRAM process (or requires one through CHIPS conditions): 1y-nm 8 Gb cell, sense amp, redundancy and test flow. It publishes this as a licensed open PDK with a reference die, so any foundry (GF, Intel, SkyWater, TI) can run DRAM wafers on spare 300 mm capacity.
why: U.S. manufacturability and the know-how chokepoint: existing logic foundries could add DRAM output in ~2 years instead of 5; 20k wafers/month adds ~3-4% to world supply.

title: Central banker's Strategic DRAM Reserve of nitrogen-stored dies
idea: Treat DRAM like oil: a federal reserve buys known-good DRAM wafers and dies in gluts, when contract prices fall below cash cost, and stores them in dry-nitrogen cabinets where dies keep for over 10 years. It auctions them to U.S. module assemblers when prices pass 2x the trailing average.
why: Supply stability and capital: damps the boom-bust cycle that deters capex; a ~5 EB reserve could cap a 4x spike, keep fabs running full through downturns, and lower every producer's cost of capital.

title: Cuban mechanic's almendron: keep old DDR4 alive behind CXL
idea: Havana mechanics keep 1950s cars running with improvised parts. In the same spirit, low-cost CXL Type-3 bridge cards each host 8-16 retired DDR4 RDIMMs and give new DDR5 servers a second-life capacity tier. The controller adds chipkill-class ECC and runs the DDR4 at reduced speed so it lasts longer.
why: Reuse supply: hyperscalers retire tens of millions of DDR4 DIMMs a year; reusing them could displace 10-20% of new DDR5 purchases for capacity-bound workloads, at ~150 ns extra latency.

title: Commodities trader's DRAM bit futures to pre-sell fab output
idea: List an exchange-traded DRAM futures and options contract, settled on a standardized 16 Gb DDR5-equivalent bit index. New entrants can then sell 3-5 years of output forward and hedge it, and lenders can underwrite fabs on hedged revenue the way they underwrite LNG terminals.
why: Capital intensity: hedged revenue could cut the equity a $15B fab needs by ~30-40% and draw in infrastructure investors who avoid commodity price risk.

title: Real-estate developer's Fab REIT leases cleanroom bays monthly
idea: A REIT owns the cleanroom shells, utilities and depreciating tools (scanners, deposition, etch) and leases 'bays' with shared metrology to DRAM startups and university spinouts on 3-36 month terms. A team can then run a 2k-wafer/month line without owning a $15B building.
why: Capital intensity and entry barriers: turns capex into opex and cuts a startup's entry cost from billions to ~$50-200M, so more DRAM approaches can reach volume.

title: Medieval guild: teaching fab whose apprentices ship real DRAM
idea: On the guild model, a state-chartered 200 mm teaching fab has apprentice technicians run a legacy DDR3/LPDDR2 product for automotive and industrial customers as their coursework, with certification after 18 months. Product revenue covers ~60% of operating cost.
why: The workforce chokepoint in U.S. manufacturability: a 40k-wafer/month fab needs ~3,000 technicians; the guild trains them while adding legacy supply that frees leading-edge capacity.

title: Chef's tapas menu: cloud memory sold in exact portions
idea: Instead of fixed 'set menus' of 4 or 8 GB per vCPU, clouds sell memory on its own in 1 GB increments backed by pooled CXL DIMMs, with pricing that rewards right-sizing. Schedulers bin-pack against measured working-set telemetry rather than requested size.
why: Doing DRAM's job with less: fixed memory-to-vCPU ratios strand ~20-30% of purchased DRAM; a la carte sizing could cut fleet DRAM demand ~15%.

title: Librarian's catalog: signed lifetime passport on every DIMM
idea: Each module's SPD carries a signed lifetime log written by the host BMC: power-on hours, thermal history, corrected-error counts, row-hammer events. Second-hand buyers can grade modules the way a library tracks a book's condition, and a public registry prices reuse by verified health.
why: Reuse supply: buyers' distrust is the main barrier to secondary DRAM markets; verified provenance could lift reuse from <10% to 40%+ of retired server DRAM.

title: Prospector reworks tailings: tungsten from fab waste and boards
idea: Like prospectors reworking old tailings, recover tungsten from WF6 exhaust scrubbers, W-CMP slurry and scrapped memory boards by electrochemical leaching and solvent extraction. The output is domestic fab-grade WF6 feedstock.
why: Scarce-resource chokepoint (China ~80% of tungsten): well under half of the WF6 fed into a chamber ends up as film, so a closed loop could cover a large share of a U.S. DRAM fab's tungsten demand.

title: Submariner's closed loop: recapture every liter of fab helium
idea: Submarines recycle everything. Fit each etch and deposition chamber's backside-cooling and leak-check helium lines with local recovery (pump-exhaust capture plus membrane and cryogenic purification) that returns 6N helium to a fab-wide loop.
why: Helium chokepoint (Qatar offline): 85-95% recapture cuts a fab's helium purchases ~10x and removes a shutdown risk.

title: Jugaad engineer's frugal 200 mm legacy DRAM line from used tools
idea: With Indian jugaad frugality, build a 200 mm line from used ArF-dry and KrF tools (~$300M) that makes 38-50 nm DDR3/LPDDR2 4 Gb parts for automotive, industrial and IoT customers whose qualified designs need legacy DRAM. That frees leading-edge wafers for dense parts.
why: Supply and capital: a $300M line instead of a $15B fab gives U.S. supply security for long-lifecycle markets and moves legacy demand off leading-edge capacity.

title: Amish barn-raising: warehouse fab with sealed tool minienvironments
idea: Raise a fab the way an Amish community raises a barn. Skip the ballroom cleanroom: each tool sits in a sealed ISO-1 minienvironment linked by sealed overhead FOUP transport inside a cheap warehouse shell that modular crews put up in ~9 months.
why: Capital intensity and time: cleanroom shells and HVAC are ~20-30% of fab capex and take 2+ years; this roughly halves both.

title: Privateer's letter of marque: advance market commitment for U.S. DRAM
idea: Governments once licensed privateers with guaranteed prize money. Here the U.S. issues an advance market commitment: federal datacenters and DoD will buy the first 2 EB of U.S.-made DRAM that meets a spec, at a guaranteed $/GB floor for 5 years, from any entrant.
why: Demand-side de-risking for U.S. manufacturability: guaranteed offtake makes new entrants bankable without the government picking technology winners.

title: Artist's new canvas: DRAM-class gain cells on display-fab glass
idea: An artist sees the world's underused Gen-8.5 display fabs as huge, cheap canvases. Pattern IGZO 2T0C gain-cell arrays at 1-2 um rules on 2.2 x 2.5 m glass, dice the glass into tiles and stack them as low-cost capacity modules for warm data.
why: Capital intensity: a whole new non-semiconductor source of capacity in fabs that process glass for ~$100-300/m^2; areal density (~3 GB/m^2) and speed at TFT rules are the weak points, so it suits bulk tiers.

title: War Production Board converts idle logic and NAND lines to DRAM
idea: As the 1942 War Production Board turned car plants into bomber lines, use the Defense Production Act to fund converting underused 300 mm logic or NAND lines (28-40 nm) to DRAM under licensed cell IP. Grants cover retooling of the capacitor and deep-etch modules.
why: Time and capital: conversion takes ~18 months at ~20% of greenfield cost because the shell, utilities and most tools already exist.

title: Archaeologist excavates know-how: rehire retired DRAM process veterans
idea: Treat process know-how as buried artifacts. A startup recruits retired DRAM integration engineers (Qimonda Richmond, Elpida and Micron Manassas alumni) into a 'reconstruction' team, digitizes their recipe notebooks, and rebuilds a 30-40 nm DRAM flow in 18 months instead of 5 years of R&D.
why: The know-how chokepoint: tacit process knowledge, more than tools, is the biggest barrier to entry; this cuts years off time-to-yield for a U.S. entrant.

title: Monk's vow of simplicity: RAM-Star label for lean software
idea: Take a monk's austerity: federal procurement adopts a 'RAM Star' certification, modeled on Energy Star, that requires software to meet memory-footprint benchmarks per workload (browsers, Java services, containers), backed by runtime guidance (compressed pointers, arena allocators, page sharing).
why: Demand reduction: software bloat drives DRAM per device; a 20-30% footprint cut across federal and enterprise fleets frees exabyte-scale supply at no fab cost.

title: Bottle-deposit grandmother: refundable deposit on every memory module
idea: Like a bottle deposit, add a refundable $2-5/GB deposit when DIMMs and LPDDR boards are sold, paid back when the module is returned to a certified refurbisher. This guarantees a steady reverse-logistics flow for harvesting and reuse.
why: Reuse supply: bottle deposits reach 80-90% return rates; capturing retired DRAM systematically could add several % to annual bit supply.

title: Venetian glassblower: continuous Czochralski with synthetic silica crucibles
idea: Murano masters guarded their furnaces. Break the Spruce Pine quartz chokepoint by pairing continuous-feed Czochralski growth (5-8 ingots per crucible, recharged with granular polysilicon) with sol-gel synthetic fused-silica inner liners made from domestic SiCl4.
why: Scarce-resource chokepoint (>80% of high-purity quartz from Spruce Pine): cuts crucible use per wafer ~5x and ends the single-site dependency.

title: Vertical farmer grows 64 crystal tiers in one epitaxy season
idea: A vertical farmer grows many layers in one season instead of buying more land. One epitaxy run deposits 64 Si/SiGe pairs; a single slit mask lets the SiGe be removed selectively, freeing 64 single-crystal Si channel tiers that are wrapped in ALD gates, with lateral ZrO2 capacitors in the space the SiGe left. U.S. epi-tool makers and a DRAM startup co-own the flow.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: 64 tiers at ~0.2x planar density each gives ~12x bits/mm^2. The tiers come from one epi run and one etch rather than 64 litho cycles, so wafer cost stays near a planar DRAM wafer's.

title: Grandparents' fabs: depreciated lines make thin array layers for bonding
idea: Retirees still work, and cheaply. Fully depreciated 300 mm fabs (28-40 nm) make array-only wafers with just 3 ArF masks and no periphery. These are thinned to 5 um and hybrid-bonded 16 deep onto one leading-edge wafer that carries all sense amps and decoders.
why: Toward the 10x constraint: 16 array layers at ~0.6x areal density each is ~10x bits per footprint. Depreciation is ~55% of wafer cost and is gone in written-off fabs, so the full stack costs ~1.5x one conventional wafer for 10x the bits (~6x lower $/bit). This misses strict same-cost, but it makes a new business for old fabs.

title: Squatter claims airspace: memory tiers in the BEOL above logic dies
idea: An urban squatter occupies unused airspace. Foundries sell a 'memory roof' option: 20 tiers of low-temperature (<400 C) ALD In2O3 2T0C gain cells built in the BEOL above accelerator and CPU logic, so die area already paid for by logic also carries DRAM-class memory and foundries become DRAM suppliers.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: at ~20F^2 per cell with F=20 nm, each tier holds ~15 MB/mm^2, so 20 tiers give ~300 MB/mm^2, ~10x a DDR5 die. The only cost is BEOL deposition, roughly one DRAM wafer's worth per logic wafer, and no separate die, package or PHY is needed.

title: Polar explorer's 77 K cold-memory pods run by gas suppliers
idea: A polar explorer knows cold preserves things. At 77 K access-transistor leakage falls by more than 10^6, so a cell needs ~0.3 fF instead of 5 fF: the 70:1 pillar gives way to a planar MIM cap over a vertical-channel 4F^2 transistor, and 7 such tiers are bonded. The pods are LN2-immersion memory, sold as a service by industrial-gas firms.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: 4F^2 vs 6F^2 (1.5x) times 7 tiers is ~10x bits/mm^2. Deleting the high-aspect-ratio capacitor module and refresh offsets the bonding and cooling cost; cryo-CMOS sensing margins are the risk.

title: Embargo engineer's ruler: ALD film thickness, not EUV, sets pitch
idea: Denied EUV, a Soviet-style engineer measures with films instead of light. ArF-defined trenches get access transistors on both sidewalls, with gate length and wordline width set by ALD film thickness (~5 nm). The sidewall cell is repeated on 2 stacked trench levels, all in mature U.S. 28-40 nm fabs.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: an effective ~5 nm F on the sidewalls gives ~5x cells/mm^2 versus 6F^2 at 12 nm, times 2 levels, ~10x. Dropping all 5-7 EUV layers keeps wafer cost flat or lower.

title: Child counting on fingers: 4-bit gain cells multiply existing fabs
idea: A child counts past ten by using more fingers per hand. Each non-destructive gain cell stores 16 current levels, read by a shared 4-bit flash ADC per 64 bitlines with per-row reference cells, and 3 tiers are bonded. A fabless memory-IP startup licenses it so existing DRAM fabs make ~4x the bits per wafer without new tools.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: 4 bits/cell times 3 tiers is ~12x bits/mm^2. Multi-level sensing adds ~10% periphery while wafer cost stays put; level margin against leakage drift is the risk.

title: Alien measures memory in entropy: sell 'effective GB' modules
idea: Aliens count entropy, not bytes. Memory makers sell CXL modules whose controller does inline ANS/LZ compression, cache-line dedup and zero-page elision, plus fabric-wide dedup of identical pages (model weights, OS images, KV-cache prefixes) across 1,000 hosts. They price per effective GB.
why: Meets the 10x constraint for AI inference fleets: 50-100 replicas hold identical weights and shared prompt prefixes, so pooled dedup plus compression gives ~10x effective bits per physical bit for ~5% controller cost. General workloads honestly see 2-3x.

title: Biologist's self-assembly: block copolymers draw 5 nm cells
idea: Cells build structures by self-assembly. High-chi silicon-containing block copolymers on sparse ArF guide patterns define a 10 nm-pitch hexagonal array of vertical nanowire access transistors, each with an oxide-semiconductor storage node instead of a capacitor. Spin-coat and anneal from U.S. chemical suppliers replace 5-7 EUV layers.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: 4F^2 at F=5 nm vs 6F^2 at 12 nm is ~8.6x; with periphery under the array, ~10x/mm^2. Spin-and-bake costs far less than EUV, so wafer cost stays flat; DSA defectivity is the big risk.

title: Fishmonger's fresh catch: 1 ms 'ephemeral DRAM' grade for AI
idea: A fishmonger sells today's catch, not frozen stock. A JEDEC 'ephemeral DRAM' grade for AI activations and KV caches, whose data lives under 1 ms, specifies 1 ms retention instead of 64 ms. Each cell can then drop from 5 fF to ~0.1 fF, a planar gate-capacitance node with no pillar, so cells shrink to 4F^2 and stack 6 thin tiers.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: capacitor-free 4F^2 cells times 6 tiers is ~9-10x/mm^2. Deleting the high-aspect-ratio capacitor module (~25-30% of process cost) pays for the tiers, and most rows are rewritten before they need refresh.

title: Plumber's check valve: two-terminal thyristor crosspoint decks on ex-Optane tools
idea: A plumber thinks in valves. A two-terminal vertical poly-Si p-n-p-n thyristor latch at each crosspoint holds a bit by regeneration, with no access transistor and no capacitor. Eight 4F^2 crosspoint decks are built in the BEOL with the process flow and tool set of the retired 3D XPoint (Optane) lines.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: 8 decks at 4F^2 vs 6F^2 is ~12x bits/mm^2. Two masks per deck on idled crosspoint tooling keep wafer cost near DRAM's; latch standby current and disturb are the risks.

title: Papermaker's book: roll-to-roll foil memory laminated 800 sheets deep
idea: A papermaker makes thick books from cheap sheets. Print single-tier oxide-TFT gain-cell memory on 10 um polyimide foil by roll-to-roll nanoimprint at ~100 nm rules, then laminate ~800 sheets per cm with anisotropic conductive film and edge-plated through-stack bus lines into a memory 'book'.
why: Meets the 10x constraint volumetrically: ~60 MB/cm^2 per sheet times 800 sheets is ~50 GB/cm^3, versus ~2 GB/cm^3 for a DIMM. Roll-to-roll costs (~$20-50/m^2 per sheet) keep cost per module flat; sheet alignment and yield are the risks.

title: Arsenal of Democracy retools NAND lines for quasi-volatile 3D NOR
idea: As Detroit retooled car lines for bombers in 1942, NAND makers retool lines now in oversupply to make quasi-volatile 3D NOR. It keeps the 200-layer stack but uses ~2-3 nm direct-tunneling charge-trap cells in a NOR arrangement, aiming for ~100 ns random access, >1e12 cycles and retention of seconds to minutes.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: inherits 3D NAND's ~10-15x areal density over DRAM at NAND-like wafer cost, with rare refresh. Endurance at thin oxide and write latency are the risks.

title: 2050 watchmaker places phosphorus atoms as multi-electron bits
idea: A 2050 watchmaker places atoms instead of gears. Hydrogen-resist STM lithography places 4-atom phosphorus donor clusters in silicon at 3 nm pitch; each cluster holds 0-3 extra electrons (2 bits), sensed by an adjacent single-electron transistor. A national atomic-precision consortium runs MEMS arrays of 10^5 STM tips to write each wafer.
why: Meets the 10x constraint with margin: 3 nm pitch is ~100x the areal density of 6F^2 at 12 nm, so even 10x periphery overhead clears 10x. Cost depends entirely on tip parallelism, and it likely needs cryogenic operation.

title: Hotel concierge: on-module DRAM front desk over flash storage
idea: A concierge keeps tonight's keys at the desk and everything else in storage. An on-module 'memory hotel' pairs 16 GB of DRAM with 256 GB of low-latency SLC flash behind a controller that predicts and prefetches hot 4 KB pages, presenting 272 GB to the host as byte-addressable CXL memory.
why: Meets the 10x constraint in capacity per module: ~10x for about the same module cost, since SLC flash is ~1/10 of DRAM's $/bit. A hot-set hit rate above 99% keeps average latency DRAM-class, but misses cost ~5-10 us and flash endurance limits write-heavy use.

title: Quilter uses whole cloth: undiced wafer-scale memory cassettes
idea: A quilter works with whole cloth. Skip dicing, packaging and DIMM PCBs: ship whole 300 mm DRAM wafers with wafer-level redundancy routing and edge contacts, stacked 20 deep in a liquid-cooled cassette that plugs into a rack CXL switch.
why: Meets the 10x constraint volumetrically: one wafer holds ~1.5-2 TB, so a 20-wafer cassette is ~35 TB in ~4 L, versus hundreds of liters of server DIMM slots. Packaging, PCB and per-die test savings (~15-20% of module cost) pay for the redundancy.

title: Pastry chef's mille-feuille: 64 tiers of 2D-semiconductor gain cells
idea: A pastry chef folds dough into hundreds of layers. Grow wafer-scale MOCVD MoS2/WSe2 monolayers (0.7 nm thick) and stack 64 transistor tiers separated by 10 nm hBN or oxide. Each tier's storage node is the gate of an ultralow-leakage 2D-channel 2T0C cell, and the whole stack is ~1 um tall. U.S. 2D-material growers become a new supply chain.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: 64 tiers at ~0.2x planar density is ~12x/mm^2. The thin tiers keep via etch aspect ratio under 20:1, so per-tier cost is small and wafer cost stays near DRAM's.

title: Mail carrier's local post offices: a sense amp every 32 cells
idea: Mail goes out from local post offices, not one central depot. Hybrid-bond a sense-amp wafer under the array so every 32 cells get their own sense amp on a ~0.05 fF micro-bitline, which cuts the charge a cell needs from ~5 fF to ~0.3 fF. The capacitor becomes a shallow planar MIM, the array shrinks to 4F^2, and 6 array decks share one sense wafer.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: 4F^2 vs 6F^2 times 6 decks is ~9-10x/mm^2. Dropping the 60-75:1 pillar etch saves ~20% of wafer cost, which pays for the bonding, and the periphery leaves the array die.

title: Rail yard master: racetrack memory built in U.S. hard-disk head fabs
idea: A rail yard master moves cars along sidings instead of building a track for each car. Magnetic domain-wall racetrack memory uses vertical U-shaped nanowires, each holding ~64 domains shifted by current past one read/write head. It is built in U.S. hard-disk read-head fabs, which already pattern 20 nm magnetic multilayers in volume and are losing HDD demand.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: 64 bits per ~4F^2 track footprint is ~10-20x DRAM areal density. The head fabs are depreciated, domain-wall motion does not wear out, and shift latency is tens of ns; pinning and shift errors are the risks.

title: Gutenberg's press: one 3D imprint stamps all 128 staircase steps
idea: Gutenberg replaced hand copying with a press. A 3D multi-level nanoimprint template, written once by e-beam, stamps all 128 staircase steps and tier contacts of a 3D DRAM stack in a single imprint, replacing ~30 litho/trim cycles. U.S. template shops and NIL tool vendors form the supply chain.
why: Meets the 10x constraint as a cost enabler: staircase and contacts are ~30-40% of a 3D memory wafer's cost, and collapsing them to one imprint lets a 128-tier 3D DRAM (~10x/mm^2) be built at about today's DRAM wafer cost.

title: Ham radio operator: 32-die stacks talk through inductive coils
idea: A ham operator talks without wires. Stack 32 thinned DRAM dies that pass data through on-die inductive coils (near-field links, ~1 pJ/bit) instead of TSVs, bonded with thin adhesive and powered by edge-plated rails. Any OSAT can assemble them on NAND-style die-stacking lines.
why: Meets the 10x constraint per package footprint: 32 dies is ~10x the bits of 2-4-high packages. Removing TSVs (HBM's ~3x area-per-bit tax and 20-30% yield loss) holds $/GB at commodity DDR level, so this is same cost per bit, not per package.

title: Astronomer's CCD loops: charge-packet memory made in image-sensor fabs
idea: An astronomer knows CCDs move charge packets almost losslessly. 'CCD-loop memory' circulates rows of 64 contactless charge buckets in short loops past one sense amp, each bucket holding a 3-bit packet, with no access transistor per bit. It is built in U.S. CMOS image-sensor fabs on a mature process.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: ~2F^2 per bucket vs 6F^2 (3x) times 3 bits per packet (3x) is ~9-10x bits/mm^2 at mature-node wafer cost. Average access is ~32 shifts x 2 ns, about 70 ns, and dark current sets the refresh rate.

title: Sculptor carves inside the block: 50 porous-silicon tiers in one wet step
idea: A sculptor carves inside the block instead of adding clay. Pulse the current while anodizing a bulk Si wafer in HF to form 50 alternating high- and low-porosity layers in one ~10-minute wet step. A hydrogen anneal reseals the low-porosity layers into single-crystal Si sheets over voids (silicon-on-nothing physics), giving a 50-tier channel stack without epitaxy.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: a wet electrochemical step costing under ~$50 per wafer replaces a $1,000+ epitaxial superlattice, so a 50-tier 3D DRAM (~10x/mm^2) keeps wafer cost flat. It needs only U.S. wet-bench suppliers and no scarce gases.

title: Chemist's electron sponges: polyoxometalate molecules as 2-bit storage nodes
idea: A chemist sees molecules that soak up electrons like sponges. Graft polyoxometalate clusters (~1 nm, reversibly holding 0-3 extra electrons at distinct potentials) as the storage node on the gate of a vertical oxide-semiconductor read transistor, so one molecule stores 2 bits with no capacitor. U.S. specialty-chemical makers supply self-limiting monolayer inks.
why: Meets the 10x constraint: no capacitor plus 2 bits per cell lets a 4F^2 vertical cell in 3 tiers reach ~9-12x bits/mm^2 at about today's wafer cost. Electron transfer is fast, but retention and stability at 85 C are unproven.
